lead: Energy changes are easy to measure and easy to misread. A reaction that releases heat can still refuse to happen. Enthalpy counts heat at constant pressure, entropy counts spreading, and free energy combines both so its sign decides direction. Industry sizes reactors and boilers with these functions; electrochemistry predicts cell voltage from free energy.
prereq: You need school-level mole concept, stoichiometry, and balanced chemical equations.

blocks.text: A system is what you study; surroundings are the rest. A closed system exchanges heat, not matter. An open system exchanges both. An isolated system exchanges neither. One visible phase is homogeneous; two or more is heterogeneous.
ΔU = q + w
blocks.where: ΔU = internal-energy change (J); q = heat added to system (J); w = work done on system (J).

blocks.text: q is positive when heat enters; w is positive when work is done on the system. U is a state function: it depends on present state, not route. q and w are path functions; q + w is fixed.
Most reactions run in open vessels at constant pressure, where expansion work PV is hidden inside enthalpy.
H = U + PV
blocks.where: H = enthalpy (J); U = internal energy (J); P = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³).

blocks.text: At constant pressure q_p = ΔH. Heat capacity is C = q/ΔT in J K⁻¹; at constant pressure q_p = C_p ΔT, so C_p = ΔH/ΔT.
The first law allows every energy-balanced change. The second law picks direction: total entropy of system plus surroundings never decreases in a spontaneous change.
ΔS = q_rev / T
blocks.where: ΔS = entropy change (J K⁻¹); q_rev = reversible heat (J); T = kelvin temperature.

blocks.text: Entropy measures how widely energy spreads. Melting, boiling, and raising gas molecules increase entropy. Molar units: J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Standard entropies S° are tabulated at 298 K and 1 bar.
ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants)
blocks.where: ΔS° = standard entropy change (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); S° = molar standard entropy.

blocks.text: ΔH° = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants)
blocks.where: ΔH° = standard enthalpy change (J); ΔH°f = standard enthalpy of formation (J mol⁻¹).

blocks.text: Bond enthalpies give rough answers; formation enthalpies give accurate ones. Rates are separate; see 3.2.
G = H − TS
blocks.where: G = Gibbs free energy (J); H = enthalpy (J); T = kelvin; S = entropy (J K⁻¹).

blocks.text: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
blocks.where: ΔG = free-energy change (J); at constant T and P, its sign decides direction.

blocks.text: ΔG < 0 means the forward reaction goes; ΔG > 0 means it does not go and the reverse does. ΔG = 0 means equilibrium. Under standard conditions ΔG° = 0 gives K = 1.
ΔG° = −RT ln K
blocks.where: R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; K = equilibrium constant; large negative ΔG° means products dominate.

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach this bridge inside thermodynamics. Cell construction stays in Unit 4.
ΔG° = −nFE°
blocks.where: n = moles electrons; F = 96500 C mol⁻¹; E° = standard cell potential (V); ΔG° in J.

blocks.text: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q
blocks.where: Q = reaction quotient. At 298 K, 2.303RT/F = 0.0592 V (and RT/F = 0.0257 V), so E = E° − (0.0592/n) log₁₀ Q.

blocks.text: Negative ΔG° gives positive E°; positive E drives current. Reduction potentials are in Unit 4.

figure.caption: Read downward: the first law fixes energy bookkeeping, enthalpy fixes constant-pressure heat, entropy fixes direction, and free energy joins temperature to both. Only the last box decides whether the reaction runs.

spec.title: From energy to spontaneity
spec.aria: A downward flow from system definitions through the first law, enthalpy and entropy to Gibbs free energy and the spontaneity condition.

examples.question: Zn(s)+Cu²⁺(aq)→Zn²⁺(aq)+Cu(s): ΔG°=−212 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Find E° and E when [Zn²⁺]=0.10 M, [Cu²⁺]=1.0 M. n=2, F=96500 C mol⁻¹. (5 marks)
steps: Q < 1, so E is slightly above E°.
examples.check:
import math
dG = -212000.0
n = 2
F = 96500.0
E0 = -dG/(n*F)
Q = 0.10/1.0
E = E0 - (0.0592/n)*math.log10(Q)
print(round(E0, 2))
print(round(Q, 2))
print(round(E, 2))

traps: Predicting from ΔH alone. ΔG decides.
Using °C in TΔS; T must be kelvin.
Mixing kJ and J in ΔH − TΔS; convert first.
Writing Q upside down; Q = products/reactants, each raised to its coefficient.
Using ΔG° when concentrations are nonstandard; Nernst gives E.

quiz.q: Define state and path functions with one example each.
quiz.a: State depends on present state: U, H, S. Path depends on route: q, w.

quiz.q: Why use ΔH for open-beaker reactions?
quiz.a: Open beakers are at constant pressure; measured heat is q_p = ΔH, which includes PV work.

quiz.q: ΔH=+58 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS=+176 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Above what T is it spontaneous?
E°=0.34 V, n=2. Find ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹.
CaCO₃(s)→CaO(s)+CO₂(g) has ΔH>0. Why strong heating?
quiz.a: ΔS>0 because gas forms. ΔG=ΔH−TΔS<0 only when TΔS>ΔH, so high T is needed.

quiz.q: Water boils at 373 K, ΔH_vap=40.7 kJ mol⁻¹. Estimate ΔS_vap.
quiz.a: ΔS = 40700/373 = 109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; large because gas is more disordered.

beyond: Not for the exam. Free energy becomes chemical potential when composition changes; this drives phase diagrams and electrochemical models. Drug design uses ΔG of binding split into enthalpy and entropy. Battery engineers track ΔG versus temperature for thermal runaway. Search next: activity coefficients, exergy analysis, isothermal titration calorimetry.
